newsitem.title: democratic republic of congo: No fuel halts output at new Congo Kolwezi mine.
newsitem.headline: No fuel halts output at new Congo Kolwezi mine.

text.p: Production at the Kolwezi copper/cobalt mine has been halted for about two weeks due to a lack of fuel said Joseph Dassas, head of the America Mineral Fields Inc (AMF) project.
He said the shortage had been triggered by the New Democratic Republic of Congo government's renationalisation of the railroad linking it to South Africa.
"There has been no production for about two weeks because of lack of fuel. There are no trucks running because there is no fuel," Dassas said.
The mine has been producing around 12,000 tonnes of copper a year. Cobalt production figures were not immediately available.
The fuel crisis had stemmed from a lack of funding from the government combined with problems with the railway lines and South African firms which are currently the only source of fuel, Dassas said.

Shortly after ousting former President Mobutu Sese Seko last month, rebel leader Laurent Kabila's new government seized control of the railroad, upsetting South African transport companies which operate trains along it.
Industry sources said South Africa had refused to send additional locomotive coaches to New Congo until the Alliance government returned 60 South African railcars it was holding.
"There has been some misunderstanding between the South Africans and the Alliance government," Dassas said.

Kasongo Tshikomba, director of former Zaire's railways, said on Wednesday the Kabila government, which has pledged a $300 million upgrade of the Shaba line, was willing to co-operate with the South Africans.
AMF's Dassas said he was unsure as to how long the fuel shortage would last, adding it depended on negotiations currently underway.
At peak production the Kolwezi mine used 6,000 cubic metres of gasoil per month, Dassas said.

AMF has signed a contract to process copper/cobalt tailings at Kolwezi. It said earlier it expected to produce 50,000 tonnes of copper a year and 6,000 tonnes of cobalt when the tailings project reaches full production in 2000.
